title: Strength of materials
note: Stress σ = F/A is internal force per area; strain ε = ΔL/L is stretch per length. In the elastic range σ = Eε (Hooke's law), and E measures stiffness. Past the yield strength a part deforms permanently; the ultimate strength is the peak of the stress-strain curve. Parts can also fail by fatigue under repeated loads or by buckling in compression.

read.title: What the tensile test tells you
text: The basic experiment of strength of materials is simple: grip a bar and pull it while measuring force and stretch. Dividing force by area gives stress, and dividing stretch by original length gives strain. Plotting one against the other gives the stress-strain curve.

At first the curve is a straight line. Stress is proportional to strain, the bar springs back fully when released, and the slope is Young's modulus, the material's stiffness. Steel's is about 200 GPa, aluminum's about 70 GPa, so an aluminum rod stretches about three times as much as an identical steel rod under the same load.

At the yield strength the line bends over and the bar begins to deform permanently. A ductile metal keeps stretching and hardening until it reaches its ultimate tensile strength, then narrows locally, or necks, and breaks. A brittle material such as glass gives almost no warning and snaps near the end of its straight line.

Two failure modes never show up in a single pull. Fatigue cracks grow under millions of load cycles well below yield, usually from a notch or sharp corner. Buckling makes a slender column bow sideways at a load set by its stiffness and length, not by its strength.
